{{short description|Formalism in classical field theory based on Hamiltonian mechanics}}
{{Classical mechanics}}
In [[theoretical physics]], '''Hamiltonian field theory''' is the field-theoretic analogue to classical [[Hamiltonian mechanics]]. It is a formalism in [[classical field theory]] alongside [[Lagrangian field theory]]. It also has applications in [[quantum field theory]].

==Definition==

The [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian]] for a system of discrete particles is a function of their [[generalized coordinates]] and conjugate momenta, and possibly, time. For continua and fields, Hamiltonian mechanics is unsuitable but can be extended by considering a large number of point masses, and taking the continuous limit, that is, infinitely many particles forming a continuum or field. Since each point mass has one or more [[degrees of freedom (physics and chemistry)|degrees of freedom]], the field formulation has infinitely many degrees of freedom.

===One scalar field===

The Hamiltonian density is the continuous analogue for fields; it is a function of the fields, the conjugate "momentum" fields, and possibly the space and time coordinates themselves. For one [[scalar field]] {{math|''φ''('''x''', ''t'')}}, the Hamiltonian density is defined from the [[Lagrangian density]] by<ref group=nb>It is a standard abuse of notation to abbreviate all the derivatives and coordinates in the Lagrangian density as follows:
:<math>\mathcal{L} (\phi, \partial_\mu \phi, x_\mu)</math>
The {{math|''μ''}} is an index which takes values 0 (for the time coordinate), and 1, 2, 3 (for the spatial coordinates), so strictly only one derivative or coordinate would be present. In general, all the spatial and time derivatives will appear in the Lagrangian density, for example in Cartesian coordinates, the Lagrangian density has the full form:
:<math>\mathcal{L} \left(\phi, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}, x,y,z,t\right)</math>
Here we write the same thing, but using ∇ to abbreviate all spatial derivatives as a vector.</ref>

:<math>\mathcal{H}(\phi, \pi, \mathbf{x},t) = \dot{\phi}\pi - \mathcal{L}(\phi, \nabla\phi, \partial \phi/\partial t , \mathbf{x},t)\,.</math>

with {{math|∇}} the [[gradient operator|"del" or "nabla" operator]], {{math|'''x'''}} is the [[position vector]] of some point in space, and {{math|''t''}} is [[time]]. The Lagrangian density is a function of the fields in the system, their space and time derivatives, and possibly the space and time coordinates themselves. It is the field analogue to the Lagrangian function for a system of discrete particles described by generalized coordinates.

As in Hamiltonian mechanics where every generalized coordinate has a corresponding generalized momentum, the field {{math|''φ''('''x''', ''t'')}} has a '''conjugate momentum field''' {{math|''π''('''x''', ''t'')}}, defined as the partial derivative of the Lagrangian density with respect to the time derivative of the field,

:<math>\pi = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot{\phi}} \,,\quad \dot{\phi}\equiv\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}\,,</math>

in which the overdot<ref group=nb>This is standard notation in this context, most of the literature does not explicitly mention it is a partial derivative. In general total and partial time derivatives of a function are not the same.</ref> denotes a [[partial derivative|''partial'']] time derivative {{math|∂/∂''t''}}, not a [[total derivative|total]] time derivative {{math|''d''/''dt''}}.

===Many scalar fields===

For many fields {{math|''φ<sub>i</sub>''('''x''', ''t'')}} and their conjugates {{math|''π<sub>i</sub>''('''x''', ''t'')}} the Hamiltonian density is a function of them all:

:<math>\mathcal{H}(\phi_1,  \phi_2, \ldots, \pi_1, \pi_2, \ldots, \mathbf{x},t)= \sum_i\dot{\phi_i}\pi_i - \mathcal{L}(\phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots \nabla\phi_1,\nabla\phi_2,\ldots, \partial \phi_1/\partial t ,\partial \phi_2/\partial t ,\ldots, \mathbf{x},t)\,.</math>

where each conjugate field is defined with respect to its field,

:<math>\pi_i(\mathbf{x},t) = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\dot{\phi}_i} \,.</math>

In general, for any number of fields, the [[volume integral]] of the Hamiltonian density gives the Hamiltonian, in three spatial dimensions:

:<math>H = \int \mathcal{H} \ d^3 x \,.</math>

The Hamiltonian density is the Hamiltonian per unit spatial volume. The corresponding [[dimensional analysis|dimension]] is [energy][length]<sup>−3</sup>, in [[SI units]] Joules per metre cubed, J m<sup>−3</sup>.

===Tensor and spinor fields===

The above equations and definitions can be extended to [[vector field]]s and more generally [[tensor field]]s and [[spinor field]]s. In physics, tensor fields describe [[boson]]s and spinor fields describe [[fermion]]s.

==Equations of motion==

The [[equations of motion]] for the fields are similar to the Hamiltonian equations for discrete particles. For any number of fields:

{{equation box 1
|indent = :
|background colour = white
|border colour =black
|border = 1
|title = '''Hamiltonian field equations'''
|equation=<math>\dot{\phi}_i = +\frac{\delta{H}}{\delta \pi_i}\,,\quad \dot{\pi}_i = - \frac{\delta{H}}{\delta \phi_i} \,, </math>
}}

where again the overdots are partial time derivatives, the [[variational derivative]] with respect to the fields

:<math>\frac{\delta H}{\delta \phi_i} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{H}}{\partial \phi_i} - \nabla\cdot \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}}{\partial (\nabla \phi_i)}  \,,</math>

with · the [[dot product]], must be used instead of simply [[partial derivative]]s.

==Phase space==

The fields {{math|''φ<sub>i</sub>''}} and conjugates {{math|''π<sub>i</sub>''}} form an infinite dimensional [[phase space]], because fields have an infinite number of degrees of freedom.

==Poisson bracket==

For two functions which depend on the fields {{math|''φ<sub>i</sub>''}} and {{math|''π<sub>i</sub>''}}, their spatial derivatives, and the space and time coordinates,

:<math> A = \int d^3 x \mathcal{A}\left(\phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots,\pi_1,\pi_2,\ldots,\nabla\phi_1,\nabla\phi_2,\ldots,\nabla\pi_1,\nabla\pi_2,\ldots,\mathbf{x},t\right)\,,</math> 
:<math> B = \int d^3 x \mathcal{B}\left(\phi_1,\phi_2,\ldots,\pi_1,\pi_2,\ldots,\nabla\phi_1,\nabla\phi_2,\ldots,\nabla\pi_1,\nabla\pi_2,\ldots,\mathbf{x},t\right)\,,</math>

and the fields are zero on the boundary of the volume the integrals are taken over, the field theoretic [[Poisson bracket]] is defined as (not to be confused with the [[anticommutator]] from quantum mechanics).<ref>{{harvnb|Greiner|Reinhardt|1996|loc=Chapter 2}}</ref>

:<math> \{A,B\}_{\phi,\pi} = \int d^3 x \sum_i \left(\frac{\delta \mathcal{A}}{\delta \phi_i}\frac{\delta \mathcal{B}}{\delta \pi_i}-\frac{\delta \mathcal{B}}{\delta \phi_i}\frac{\delta \mathcal{A}}{\delta \pi_i}\right)\,,</math>

where <math> \delta \mathcal{F}/\delta f </math> is the [[variational derivative]]
:<math> \frac{\delta \mathcal{F}}{\delta f} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{F}}{\partial f} - \sum_i \nabla_i \frac{\partial \mathcal{F}}{\partial (\nabla_i f)} \,.</math>

Under the same conditions of vanishing fields on the surface, the following result holds for the time evolution of {{math|''A''}} (similarly for {{math|''B''}}):

:<math>\frac{dA}{dt} = \{A,H\} + \frac{\partial A}{\partial t}</math>

which can be found from the total time derivative of {{math|''A''}}, [[integration by parts]], and using the above Poisson bracket.

==Explicit time-independence==

The following results are true if the Lagrangian and Hamiltonian densities are explicitly time-independent (they can still have implicit time-dependence via the fields and their derivatives),

===Kinetic and potential energy densities===

The Hamiltonian density is the total energy density, the sum of the kinetic energy density (<math>\mathcal{T}</math>) and the potential energy density (<math>\mathcal{V}</math>),

:<math>\mathcal{H} = \mathcal{T}+\mathcal{V}\,.</math>

===Continuity equation===

Taking the partial time derivative of the definition of the Hamiltonian density above, and using the [[chain rule]] for [[implicit differentiation]] and the definition of the conjugate momentum field, gives the [[continuity equation]]:

:<math>\frac{\partial\mathcal{H}}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot \mathbf{S}=0</math>

in which the Hamiltonian density can be interpreted as the energy density, and

:<math>\mathbf{S} = \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial(\nabla\phi)}\frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t}</math>

the energy flux, or flow of energy per unit time per unit surface area.

==Relativistic field theory==
'''Covariant Hamiltonian field theory''' is the [[theory of relativity|relativistic]] formulation of Hamiltonian field theory.

Hamiltonian field theory usually means the symplectic [[Hamiltonian system|Hamiltonian formalism]] when applied to [[classical field theory]], that takes the form of the instantaneous Hamiltonian formalism on an infinite-dimensional [[phase space]], and where [[canonical coordinates]] are field functions at some instant of time.<ref>Gotay, M., A multisymplectic framework for classical field theory and the calculus of variations. II. Space + time decomposition, in "Mechanics, Analysis and Geometry: 200 Years after Lagrange" (North Holland, 1991).</ref> This Hamiltonian formalism is applied to [[quantum field theory|quantization of fields]], e.g., in quantum [[gauge theory]]. In Covariant Hamiltonian field theory,  [[canonical momenta]] ''p<sup>μ</sup><sub>i</sub>'' corresponds to derivatives of fields with respect to all world coordinates ''x<sup>μ</sup>''.<ref>Giachetta, G., Mangiarotti, L., [[Gennadi Sardanashvily|Sardanashvily, G.]], "Advanced Classical Field Theory", World Scientific, 2009, {{ISBN|978-981-283-895-7}}.</ref> Covariant Hamilton equations are equivalent to the [[Lagrangian system | Euler–Lagrange equations]] in the case of hyperregular [[Lagrangian system | Lagrangians]]. Covariant Hamiltonian field theory is developed in the Hamilton–De Donder,<ref>Krupkova, O., Hamiltonian field theory, J. Geom. Phys. '''43''' (2002) 93.</ref> polysymplectic,<ref>Giachetta, G., Mangiarotti, L., [[Gennadi Sardanashvily|Sardanashvily, G.]], Covariant Hamiltonian equations for field theory, J. Phys. '''A32''' (1999) 6629; {{arXiv|hep-th/9904062}}.</ref> multisymplectic<ref>Echeverria-Enriquez, A., Munos-Lecanda, M., Roman-Roy, N., Geometry of multisymplectic Hamiltonian first-order field theories, J. Math. Phys. '''41''' (2002) 7402.</ref> and ''k''-symplectic<ref>Rey, A., Roman-Roy, N. Saldago, M., Gunther's formalism (''k''-symplectic formalism) in classical field theory: Skinner-Rusk approach and the evolution operator, J. Math. Phys. '''46''' (2005) 052901.</ref> variants. A phase space of covariant Hamiltonian field theory is a finite-dimensional [[symplectic manifold|polysymplectic]] or [[symplectic manifold|multisymplectic]] manifold.

[[Non-autonomous mechanics|Hamiltonian non-autonomous mechanics]] is formulated as covariant Hamiltonian field theory on [[fiber bundles]] over the time axis, i.e. the [[real line]] <math>\mathbb{R}</math>.
